title: The Reclaimer
passages:
The ore stub smelled of cold iron and old brake dust. Rhea had the torch singing against the cradle bolts, blue-white sparks falling into the ballast between ties, while Teodoro held the work light steady with one hand and his tablet in the other, the screen washed out by the flare.

"Third bolt's seized," she said, not looking up. "Penetrant's been on it twenty minutes. If it snaps, we're drilling it out and that's an hour we don't have."

Teodoro tapped the manifest. "Manifest says the pod weighs four hundred twelve kilos. Cradle's rated for six. We cut it loose, the shop hoist takes the weight. No reason to rush the bolt."

"Reason is Ivo's filter alarm starts at oh-six-hundred. Reason is the water truck comes at oh-five-thirty and if the board's not clear, it turns around." She killed the torch, wiped her face with the back of a glove. "Give me the breaker bar."

He handed it over, and she set the jaw, braced a boot on the cradle flange, and leaned. Metal groaned. The bolt let go with a crack like a rifle shot.

"Two more," she said. "Then we roll the pod into the back bay and I can look at the diaphragm again before shift change."

A vibration came up through the rails, low and heavy, not the ghost trains' electric hum. Diesel, big-block, laboring up the grade. No transponder chirp cut the node's ambient chatter. No headlights swept the stub until the last ten meters, when twin beams snapped on and washed out the work light, the ties, Rhea's boots.

Teodoro shielded his tablet. "Service rig. Heavy. No ID broadcast."

The engine died. Air brakes hissed. A door clanged shut, and footsteps crunched ballast — slow, easy, like the man had nowhere urgent to be.

Rhea straightened, breaker bar resting on her shoulder. Teodoro stepped beside her, light lowered.

The man was lean, gray coveralls with the reclaimer's badge stitched dull on the chest: a stylized hook over a line. Late thirties, maybe. Hair cut short. Hands clean. He stopped three meters out, close enough to read the pod's stenciled numbers, far enough to keep his options open.

"Morning," he said. Voice pleasant, flat. "Who signs for ballast at Anza?"

Behind him, his rig's deck carried an empty cradle. Sized for exactly one box. The locking pins were already swung open.

Pell didn't smile. He reached into his coverall chest pocket and withdrew a stub of yellow brass, punched clean through with a node seal he didn't bother to hide. He walked past them to the relay counter — the steel desk bolted to the shop wall, screen dark until he woke it with a tap — and laid the token down like a bet.

"Warrant-token," he said. "Issued Kettering Central, 03:14 local. Derelict discrepancy, pod class, ballast designation. Node Anza is named."

Teodoro didn't hesitate. He set the work light on the counter, picked up the tablet, and read the token's code straight onto the board. His fingers moved the way they moved for shift logs: *manifest, confirm, enter.* The screen flickered. The board accepted it.

Then the board froze.

Shift slots grayed out one by one, names dimming to placeholder dashes. The resupply flag at the top corner flipped from GREEN to HOLD in a way that felt audible. The ambient chatter of the node — the low hum of scheduled rigs, the quiet tick of countdown timers — cut out.

Teodoro looked at the screen. His voice was flat, the same tone he used for shift changes. "Board's locked. No slot assignments. No resupply window. Water-and-parts truck at the north gate just got the hold signal."

Rhea's breaker bar dipped. "Ivo's spare scrubber cartridge is on that truck."

Teodoro nodded once. "Was. It's turning around now."

The inner door banged open. Nour stood there in her Shift 1 coveralls, clipboard in hand, the early light behind her making a silhouette of the broad shoulders and the set jaw. She looked at the board, then at Pell, then at Teodoro.

"My crew," she said. "Their names are gone. The whole day's wiped."
